## HYPOTHESIS  
X (specific structural property): Uniform loss weighting across imbalanced multi-task RL training  
Y (measurable effect, direction + magnitude): Zero-shot accuracy on underrepresented tasks drops by approximately 25% or more when dominant task frequency is at least double  
Z (quantitative causal mechanism, must predict T): Gradient norm contributions from each task scale proportionally to training sample frequency \( f_i \), so the dominant task with frequency ratio \( r = \frac{f_{\max}}{f_i} \) contributes ~\( r \) times larger gradient norm, biasing parameter updates and causing underrepresented task accuracy to degrade roughly by \(\frac{r-1}{r} \times\) baseline zero-shot accuracy.  
T (threshold with derivation): T=2 because when \( r \geq 2 \), the dominant task’s gradient norm contribution exceeds 50% of total gradient norm, predicting at least a 25% zero-shot accuracy drop on underrepresented tasks.  
Falsified if: per-task gradient norm ratio \( r > 2 \) correlates with less than 10% zero-shot accuracy drop on underrepresented tasks on Meta-World under inverse-frequency weighting control.

## METHOD  
Core component: Frequency-normalized task loss weighting module (FNTL) integrated into Multi-Task Learning from Demonstrations (MT-LfD)  
Operationalizes Z by: scaling each task’s loss inversely proportional to its training sample frequency \( f_i \), thereby normalizing per-task gradient norm contributions and directly addressing gradient imbalance predicted by Z  
Differs from B because Z implies: baseline MT-LfD’s uniform loss weighting allows gradient norms to be dominated by frequent tasks, causing biased parameter updates and degraded zero-shot generalization on underrepresented tasks, which FNTL structurally prevents by rebalancing gradients  
Intermediate Z-confirmation measurement: per-task gradient norm ratio (dominant to underrepresented) after backward pass, measured before and after applying FNTL

## EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURE  
Primary test: manipulate task loss weighting (uniform vs inverse-frequency), measure per-task gradient norm ratio and zero-shot accuracy on underrepresented tasks, expect zero-shot accuracy improvement ≥ 25% with reduced gradient norm ratio near 1 under inverse-frequency weighting if Z is true  
Control C manipulation: apply inverse-frequency normalized task loss weighting during multi-task RL training to equalize expected per-task gradient contributions  
Z predicts in C: zero-shot accuracy on underrepresented tasks increases by ≥ 25%, correlating with gradient norm ratio reduction from >2 to ~1  
Z' predicts in C: minimal zero-shot accuracy improvement (<10%) despite normalized gradient norms due to persistent representational entanglement unrelated to gradient magnitude imbalance  
Held constant: dataset, network architecture, training hyperparameters, and sampling protocols to isolate effect of loss weighting

## DATASETS  
Primary D: Meta-World benchmark — Z operative because tasks are sampled with highly imbalanced frequencies, creating the gradient norm imbalance scenario Z describes  
Additional 1: DMControl suite multi-task variant — Z more operative under synthetic frequency skews, enabling controlled tests of gradient imbalance  
Additional 2: Atari multi-game benchmark — Z less operative due to more uniform task sampling and performance degradation dominated by representational interference

## BASELINES  
Primary B: MT-LfD with uniform loss weighting — cannot exploit Z because it does not correct gradient norm imbalance caused by unequal task frequencies  
Additional 1: Multi-task SAC with prioritized experience replay — cannot exploit Z because replay prioritization does not guarantee balanced gradient norm contributions across tasks  
Additional 2: Single-task specialists ensemble — avoids multi-task gradient interference and imbalance but lacks ability to generalize zero-shot across tasks

## SUCCESS CRITERION  
Primary: per-task gradient norm ratio > T=2 correlates with zero-shot accuracy drop ≥ 25% on underrepresented tasks on Meta-World  
Derivation: because \( r=\frac{f_{\max}}{f_i} \geq 2 \) implies dominant task gradient norm >50% total, causing parameter update bias and accuracy degradation \(\approx \frac{r-1}{r}\) or ≥25%  
Z-active confirmation: per-task gradient norm ratio reduces from >2 to ~1 under FNTL, coinciding with recovery of zero-shot accuracy on underrepresented tasks by ≥25%

## FALSIFICATION EXPERIMENT  
Z predicts: applying inverse-frequency loss weighting reduces gradient norm ratio from >2 to ~1 and increases zero-shot accuracy on underrepresented tasks by ≥25%  
Z' predicts: despite gradient norm ratio reduction, zero-shot accuracy improves less than 10% due to representational entanglement persisting  
Abandon Z if: gradient norm ratio remains >2 yet zero-shot accuracy drop on underrepresented tasks is <10% on Meta-World under inverse-frequency loss weighting control

=== MECHANISM STATEMENT ===  
Z (one sentence, must include a quantitative prediction): Uniform loss weighting across state-action pairs during offline RL training causes gradient updates to be dominated by frequent states, resulting in at least a \((r-1)/r\) proportionate performance drop on rare states where \(r = \frac{f_{common}}{f_{rare}}\), predicting approximately 90% degradation for a 10x visitation frequency imbalance.  
T (numeric value + derivation in format 'T=[value] because Z predicts [step-by-step argument]'): T=10 because Z predicts that when common states appear 10 times more frequently than rare states (i.e., \(r=10\)), gradients are dominated by common states and rare state policy accuracy drops by \(\frac{(10-1)}{10} = 0.9\) or 90%.  
Z' (best alternative mechanism, one sentence, must name a structural reason): Z' posits that zero-shot generalization degradation is primarily due to insufficient representation capacity failing to disentangle rare states structurally, rather than gradient magnitude imbalance.  
Distinguishing prediction: Z predicts that reweighting loss inversely proportional to state visitation frequency (control C) will restore rare state performance significantly, whereas Z' predicts minimal improvement since representation capacity bottlenecks generalization regardless of loss weighting.

=== METHOD ===  
Core component (name the specific algorithm/loss/module): Inverse Visitation Frequency Weighted Behavior Cloning (IVF-BC) loss  
How it operationalizes Z (not 'it performs better' — the structural link to Z): The IVF-BC loss scales the MSE loss for each state-action pair by the inverse of its empirical visitation frequency, directly counteracting gradient domination by frequent states, thereby balancing gradient contributions across rare and common states.  
Structural difference from baseline B (what Z implies B cannot do): Baseline B uses uniform MSE loss causing disproportionate gradient magnitude favoring common states, which IVF-BC structurally corrects by reweighting to equalize gradient influence.  
Intermediate measurement confirming Z is active (must differ from primary metric M): Distribution of gradient norms per state visitation frequency bucket, showing balanced gradient magnitudes after weighting compared to skewed gradients in baseline.

=== DATASETS ===  
Primary: D4RL HalfCheetah-medium-replay — Z operative because this dataset exhibits large visitation frequency imbalances between common and rare states, enabling empirical gradient dominance effects predicted by Z.  
Additional 1: D4RL Hopper-medium-replay — Z more operative because Hopper exhibits similar but slightly less skewed visitation frequency distributions, allowing testing of Z under moderated imbalance.  
Additional 2: D4RL Walker2d-medium-replay — Z less operative because visitation frequency distribution is more uniform, thus less gradient dominance expected, serving as a near-negative control.

=== BASELINES ===  
Primary: Behavior Cloning with uniform MSE loss — cannot exploit Z because it does not reweight losses and thus allows gradient magnitude imbalance to degrade rare state performance.  
Additional 1: Prior Offline RL methods with learned weighting heuristics — cannot exploit Z because weighting heuristics are not explicitly or accurately aligned with visitation frequency, failing to balance gradients precisely.  
Additional 2: Contrastive representation learning approaches — cannot exploit Z because they address representation quality but do not address gradient imbalance caused by sample frequency in the loss function.

=== DISCRIMINATING EXPERIMENT ===  
Manipulation in control C: Reweight the offline RL loss inversely proportional to empirical state visitation frequencies during training.  
Z predicts (direction + magnitude): Rare state policy return improves by at least 70% relative to baseline uniform loss, substantially reducing performance gap between rare and common states.  
Z' predicts (direction + magnitude): Minimal or no significant improvement (<20%) in rare state policy return despite reweighting, since structural representation bottlenecks remain.  
Result that forces abandoning Z: Rare state policy return improves less than 20% after reweighting on D4RL HalfCheetah-medium-replay, contradicting predicted >70% recovery.

=== SUCCESS CRITERION ===  
Primary threshold: T=10 on metric M=policy return ratio (rare/common states) on dataset D=D4RL HalfCheetah-medium-replay  
Derivation: Given \(r=10\), Z predicts \(\frac{(r-1)}{r} = 0.9\) degradation in rare state accuracy; thus, uniform loss weighting will show ~90% performance drop in rare states relative to common states. Reweighting should restore at least 70% of this loss.  
Intermediate confirmation: Gradient norm distribution skew = balanced (within ±10%) after applying inverse visitation frequency weighting confirms Z active.

=== FALSIFICATION ===  
Falsified if: Rare state policy return degradation under uniform loss weighting < 30% on D4RL HalfCheetah-medium-replay under baseline behavior cloning training.

Y (measurable effect, direction + magnitude): Pearson correlation \( r \) between pLDDT and experimentally measured \(\Delta\Delta G\) stability changes declines linearly by approximately 0.1 per 5% increase in amino acid substitution beyond 15% substitutions, reaching below 0.5 at >25% substitutions

=== METHOD ===  
Core component (name the specific algorithm/loss/module): Flexibility-Calibrated Stability Prediction (FlexCaSP) module integrating predicted backbone fluctuation metrics with ΔΔG prediction.  
How it operationalizes Z (not 'it performs better' — the structural link to Z): FlexCaSP explicitly models the relationship between local predicted backbone variance (derived from AlphaFold’s internal predicted aligned error maps and pLDDT variance) and energetic destabilization by weighting mutation ΔΔG predictions by local flexibility estimates, addressing the underestimation of energy changes due to flexible regions.

text:
## HYPOTHESIS  
X (specific structural property): Fixed dropout rate \(p\) during Monte Carlo Dropout inference  
Y (measurable effect, direction + magnitude): Systematic underestimation of epistemic uncertainty variance \(\sigma^2\) for out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs by approximately 36%  
Z (quantitative causal mechanism, must predict T): The effective ensemble size of Monte Carlo Dropout scales inversely with the dropout rate \(p\), causing the predictive epistemic uncertainty variance \(\sigma^2\) to be underestimated proportionally to \((1-p)^2\); with typical \(p=0.2\), the variance is only ~64% of the true posterior variance, missing ~36%, thus predicting a threshold \(T\) for meaningful underestimation.  
T (threshold with derivation): T=0.16 because Z predicts with fixed dropout rate \(p=0.2\), the uncertainty variance capture is \((1-p)^2 = 0.8^2=0.64\), meaning a 36% underestimation; conservatively, a threshold of 16% difference in uncertainty variance ratio between in-distribution and OOD inputs is set to confirm this effect.  
Falsified if: difference in uncertainty variance ratio (OOD vs. in-distribution) between fixed and adaptive dropout < 0.16 on MNIST/notMNIST under adaptive dropout control condition.

## METHOD  
Core component: Adaptive Monte Carlo Dropout with input-dependent dropout rate scheduling via uncertainty-aware controller module  
Operationalizes Z by: Dynamically adjusting dropout rate \(p\) per input to increase effective ensemble size for high-uncertainty (OOD) inputs, mitigating variance underestimation caused by fixed \(p\) in baseline MC Dropout  
Differs from B because Z implies: Baseline MC Dropout with fixed dropout rate \(p\) cannot increase effective ensemble size per input, limiting epistemic uncertainty variance estimation and causing systematic underestimation  
Intermediate Z-confirmation measurement: Measured effective ensemble size \(1/p\) increasing by ≥30% for high-uncertainty (especially OOD) inputs compared to in-distribution inputs under adaptive dropout

## EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURE  
Primary test: manipulate dropout rate (fixed \(p=0.2\) vs. adaptive \(p\) per input), measure uncertainty variance ratio (OOD/in-distribution), expect an increase ≥0.16 if Z true  
Control C manipulation: fix dropout rate \(p=0.2\) but increase number of MC dropout samples per input (ensemble size) to isolate effect of ensemble size from dropout rate adaptation  
Z predicts in C: uncertainty variance ratio remains within ±0.05 of baseline (no significant change), as fixed \(p\) limits ensemble diversity regardless of sample count  
Z' predicts in C: uncertainty variance ratio improves significantly with increased MC samples, indicating calibration errors unrelated to dropout rate adaptation  
Held constant: model architecture, training procedure, dataset splits, number of forward passes per sample (except for sample count manipulation in control C)

## DATASETS  
Primary D: MNIST — Z operative because fixed \(p\) dropout underestimates OOD uncertainty on notMNIST as OOD dataset  
Additional 1: CIFAR-10 — Z operative because fixed dropout underestimates epistemic uncertainty on CIFAR-100 as OOD  
Additional 2: SVHN — Z less operative because natural domain shift causes different uncertainty calibration dynamics, weakening fixed \(p\) dropout variance underestimation effect

## BASELINES  
Primary B: MC Dropout with fixed \(p=0.2\) — cannot exploit Z because fixed dropout rate limits effective ensemble diversity per input  
Additional 1: Deep Ensembles — cannot exploit Z because uncertainty is captured via independently trained models, not via dropout rate adaptation  
Additional 2: Bayesian Neural Networks (variational inference) — cannot exploit Z because uncertainty is captured via learned weight distributions, independent of dropout dropout rate \(p\)

## SUCCESS CRITERION  
Primary: uncertainty variance ratio (OOD vs. in-distribution) difference > T=0.16 on MNIST/notMNIST when comparing adaptive dropout to fixed dropout baseline  
Derivation: Because Z predicts variance underestimation as \((1-p)^2=0.64\) for \(p=0.2\), missing ~36%, a conservative threshold of 16% difference confirms significant mitigation of underestimation by adaptive dropout  
Z-active confirmation: effective ensemble size \(1/p\) increases by ≥30% for OOD inputs compared to in-distribution inputs under adaptive dropout control

## FALSIFICATION EXPERIMENT  
Z predicts: In the control condition fixing \(p=0.2\) but increasing MC dropout samples, uncertainty variance ratio changes by less than ±0.05, i.e., no significant improvement  
Z' predicts: Same control condition produces a significant increase (>0.16)

## HYPOTHESIS  
X (specific structural property): Use of fixed uniform dropout probability \( p \) across all layers  
Y (measurable effect, direction + magnitude): Underestimation of predictive uncertainty by at least 20% when \( p > 0.5 \)  
Z (quantitative causal mechanism, must predict T): Applying a fixed uniform dropout probability \( p \) uniformly reduces effective network capacity across all layers, causing Monte Carlo dropout predictive variance to scale approximately as \((1-p)\). Thus, with fixed \( p \), predictive uncertainty estimates are biased downward by roughly the factor \((1-p)\) relative to the true Bayesian posterior variance, predicting a threshold for meaningful underestimation.  
T (threshold with derivation): \( T=0.8 \) because Z predicts variance scales as \((1-p)\); for \( p=0.5 \), variance is halved (0.5), so the predictive variance ratio vs. deep ensembles is expected ≈ 0.5, which is below 0.8, indicating >20% uncertainty underestimation.  
Falsified if: ratio of predictive variance (MC dropout with layerwise adaptive \( p_i \) to deep ensembles) ≥ 0.8 on CIFAR-10 under layerwise adaptive dropout training.

## METHOD  
Core component: Layerwise adaptive Monte Carlo dropout with learned dropout probabilities \( p_i \) per layer  
Operationalizes Z by: Allowing non-uniform dropout probabilities per layer enables testing whether uniform capacity reduction causes variance scaling bias; heterogeneous \( p_i \) relax uniform capacity assumptions and should reduce bias if Z holds  
Differs from B because Z implies: Baseline B uses fixed uniform dropout probability \( p \), enforcing uniform capacity scaling and thus systematically underestimating predictive variance  
Intermediate Z-confirmation measurement: Layerwise dropout variance profiles showing variance inversely proportional to \((1-p_i)\) and greater heterogeneity in adaptive dropout versus fixed uniform dropout

## EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURE  
Primary test: manipulate dropout scheme (fixed uniform \( p=0.5 \) vs. layerwise adaptive \( p_i \)), measure ratio of predictive variance (MC dropout / deep ensembles), expect ratio to increase from ≈0.5 to >0.8 if Z is true  
Control C manipulation: Implement two dropout regimes — (a) fixed uniform \( p \), (b) layerwise adaptive \( p_i \) optimized during training to maximize uncertainty calibration  
Z predicts in C: Predictive variance ratio increases by at least 30%, exceeding 0.8 under adaptive dropout  
Z' predicts in C: Predictive variance ratio remains near or below 0.5 under adaptive dropout, showing minimal improvement  
Held constant: Dataset (CIFAR-10), number of MC samples, ensemble size, training epochs, optimization hyperparameters

## DATASETS  
Primary D: CIFAR-10 — Z operative because moderate complexity reveals layerwise uncertainty differences and capacity scaling effects  
Additional 1: SVHN — Z more operative because domain shift may amplify layerwise capacity miscalibration  
Additional 2: MNIST — Z less operative because simpler data with fewer layers meaningfully contributing uncertainty reduces uniform dropout scaling impact

## BASELINES  
Primary B: MC Dropout with fixed \( p=0.5 \) — cannot exploit Z because uniform dropout enforces uniform capacity scaling and underestimates variance  
Additional 1: Deep Ensembles — cannot exploit Z because they do not rely on dropout-induced capacity scaling  
Additional 2: Bayesian Neural Networks (variational inference) — cannot exploit Z because uncertainty modeled via weight distributions, not fixed dropout rates

Z (one sentence, must include a quantitative prediction): The L2 norm of weight vectors in overparameterized Bayesian Neural Networks grows proportionally to the parameter-to-sample ratio (p/n), causing the posterior weight variance to shrink approximately as 1/(p/n), which leads to an underestimation of epistemic uncertainty and overconfident predictive distributions by a factor proportional to (p/n).  

T (numeric value + derivation in format 'T=[value] because Z predicts [step-by-step argument]'):  
T=2 because Z predicts that when p/n > 2, the posterior variance of weights collapses below half (1/2) of its ideal magnitude, leading to predictive uncertainty being underestimated by at least a factor of two, marking a threshold beyond which epistemic uncertainty is significantly compromised.  

Z' (best alternative mechanism, one sentence, must name a structural reason): The main cause of overconfident uncertainty estimates is not weight norm explosion but rather the structural mis-specification of the Bayesian prior leading to posterior collapse in certain weight subspaces, independent of overparameterization magnitude.  

Distinguishing prediction:  
Z predicts that in control C (reduced-parameter BNN with matched training data), the posterior weight variance and predictive uncertainty remain well-calibrated due to smaller p/n ratio; Z' predicts that even in control C, posterior collapse and overconfident predictions persist due to prior mis-specification regardless of parameter count.  

=== METHOD ===  
Core component (name the specific algorithm/loss/module): Variational Bayesian Neural Network with explicit weight norm monitoring and parameter count adjustment.  

How it operationalizes Z (not 'it performs better' — the structural link to Z): The method explicitly tracks the L2 norms of weight vectors and their posterior variances as a function of p/n during training, linking overparameterization to variance collapse predicted by Z.  

Structural difference from baseline B (what Z implies B cannot do): Baseline B (standard BBB) cannot prevent or detect the collapse of posterior variance driven by weight norm explosion since it lacks mechanisms to control or monitor the scaling effect of p/n on weight norms and posterior dispersion.  

Intermediate measurement confirming Z is active (must differ from primary metric M): The ratio of empirical posterior weight variance to prior variance as a monotonic decreasing function of p/n, measured across layers.

Primary: CIFAR-10 — Z operative because it provides a fixed sample size n with standard model parameterizations p that can be systematically increased to achieve p/n > 2, enabling the observation of norm explosion effects on posterior variance.
